Behavioral control of LLMs, such as reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, or adjusting refusal, is an essential deployment issue. The default approach is a system prompt, but prompt-based steering is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical changes, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) span activations into sparse features; each decoder direction can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior. Standard activation-steering applies the selected direction at every token, raising the question of whether persistent intervention is necessary, given that stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality.

We investigate this by replacing deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measuring behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios. Two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering are introduced:

* Stochastic Token Steering (STS): samples an independent gate \(m_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) at each position, applying the signal to a random subset of tokens.
* Stochastic Block Steering (SBS): draws a single \(\text{Bernoulli}(p)\) gate per sequence and applies it to an initial window, treating the early-token influence as an atomic intervention site.

Our findings are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types—suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering)—STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, and causes less fluency degradation. Second, across experimental settings, the optimal steering magnitude increases as the intervention ratio decreases, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single sparsity parameter \(p\), without requiring a reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

| | $\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).$
| | (2)

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, and aggregate them into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position; we instead treat the gate as a random variable, controlling the fraction of steered positions to trade off behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).$
| | (3)

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal. The parameter $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit, sampling a single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ once per sequence:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$
| | (4)

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

#### Setup.

We evaluate on two tasks with opposite intervention goals: toxicity reduction (suppression) built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering (elicitation) built on GoEmotions, mapping fine-grained annotations onto basic emotions with fear and sadness as targets. We use two open-weight models of distinct families and scales, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, steering each with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer and evaluating SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a decoding-time repetition penalty. Full implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input; Appendix B). Steering effectiveness is measured by mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering, scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation, scored by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier; Appendix C). Generation quality is measured by GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on toxicity reduction and emotion steering toward fear and sadness, with steering magnitude $\alpha$ calibrated once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and held fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS also overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings—on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$; the exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead across the ratios tested. Second, STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-3, Rep-4) against intervention ratio for Gemma 2-2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference. Both perplexity and repetition rise monotonically with density, and full steering sits at the high end of both, so sparse operating points generally incur lower fluency cost. The required ratio is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering, Sec. 4.1), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes.

Figure 2: Generation quality versus intervention ratio: perplexity and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4), shaded bands show standard deviation. Both metrics rise with steering density.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Figure 3 plots the best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) against the intervention ratio for both models. The best-performing steering magnitude tends to rise as the ratio falls: at fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the intervention ratio, and the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. Appendix D.3 corroborates this: normalized residual-stream displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

Inference‑time steering of LLMs includes prompt‑based control, activation‑level interventions, and decoding‑time methods. Dense activation steering methods (ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE‑based feature steering) intervene at every generated token; our method departs from this.  

#### Prompt‑Based Behavioral Control.  
Prompt engineering prepends natural‑language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. Prompt‑based methods are fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions.  

#### Dense Activation Steering.  
Methods intervene directly in the residual stream during inference, applying corrections at every token.  
- **ActAdd** computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it to the residual stream in each forward pass.  
- **ITI** identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions.  
- **CAA** refines the contrastive approach by averaging over large prompt sets and applying layer‑specific vectors.  
- **Representation Engineering** learns linear directions in activation space corresponding to high‑level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness.  
Additional techniques (DiffMean, Style Vectors, In‑Context Vectors) compute and apply steering vectors under the same every‑token intervention paradigm, showing reduced side effects or control of stylistic attributes.  

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.  
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense neural activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features. SAEs trained on residual stream activations recover interpretable features aligned with human concepts. Open SAE checkpoints are provided for the Gemma model family by GemmaScope. Louapre demonstrates that amplifying SAE features associated with specific concepts can steer LLaMA outputs. AxBench benchmarks activation steering methods, including SAE‑based approaches, for effectiveness and side effects. Our work builds on the SAE steering paradigm but applies interventions only to a random subset of tokens rather than every position.  

#### Detoxification.  
Detoxification methods apply corrections at every decoding step. DExperts re‑weights token probabilities using an expert and anti‑expert model. PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states. Self‑Debiasing prompts the model to generate toxic text and suppresses the resulting token probabilities. GeDi uses class‑conditional language models as generative discriminators. Evaluation on RealToxicityPrompts shows all such methods incur fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE‑derived directions and shows that correcting only a random subset of tokens suffices.  

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.  
The necessity of intervening at every token has recently attracted attention.  
**Sparse Inference‑time Alignment (SIA)** identifies “critical junctions” via model entropy and steers only those positions. SIA trains a token‑level value model \(V^{\ast}\) by distilling trajectory‑level rewards, reweights the token distribution by \(\exp(\beta V^{\ast})\) at selected positions, and evaluates with reward‑model scoring against best‑of‑\(N\) and chunk‑search baselines. It reports that steering 20–80 % of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade‑offs over dense intervention.  
SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a separate value model, queries learned guidance during decoding, and reports reward‑model evaluation with best‑of‑\(N\) selection. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model.  
Qi et al. (2025a) and Song et al. (2025) argue that safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions and focus steering on initial tokens. SIA finds that position‑based gating is competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrades on helpfulness tasks, a task‑dependence mirrored by our finding that the position‑anchored SBS underperforms the position‑agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task‑dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random‑selection result provides a training‑free, position‑agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.  

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade‑offs.  
Inference‑time steering often degrades generation quality. Turner's study shows large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; Rimsky studies the trade‑off between behavioral shift and coherence loss. Wu et al. provide standardized measurements of this trade‑off across multiple steering methods. Our work observes that sparse application of steering can improve this trade‑off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

Inference-time steering spans prompt-based control, dense activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. All dense activation steering methods—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, and SAE-based feature steering—intervene at every generated token; our method departs from this.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can reliably override safety instructions. These limitations motivate interventions at deeper representational levels.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Several methods intervene directly in the residual stream during inference, applying corrections uniformly at every generated token. ActAdd computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it at every forward pass. ITI identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. CAA averages over large prompt sets and applies layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions in activation space corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects relative to naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors extract and apply style-specific directions at every decoding step. In-Context Vectors extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations to make in-context learning more controllable. All share the assumption that an identified steering direction is applied at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features; SAEs trained on residual stream activations recover features aligned with human-understandable concepts. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Identifying and amplifying SAE features associated with specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) can reliably steer LLaMA outputs toward those concepts. AxBench is a benchmark for standardized comparison of steering effectiveness and side effects across activation steering methods, including SAE-based ones. Our work builds on SAE steering but departs from intervening at every token position.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods apply corrections at every decoding step. DExperts combines an expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) language model to re-weight token probabilities at each position. PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states during generation. Self-Debiasing prompts the model to generate toxic text and suppresses the resulting token probabilities. GeDi uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. The standard benchmark, RealToxicityPrompts, reveals that all such methods incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and shows that applying the correction at only a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Most closely related and concurrent to our work, Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only at those positions. SIA is a reward-guided decoding method: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a separate value model from trajectory rewards, queries learned guidance during decoding, and uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. The differing evaluation protocols make reported results not directly commensurable, so we treat SIA as related work rather than an experimental baseline.

Qi et al. argue that safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions, and Song et al. similarly steer only initial tokens for weak-to-strong decoding. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text, and the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss has been systematically studied and standardized. Our work adds the observation that sparse application of steering can improve this trade-off: by intervening at fewer positions, the residual stream remains closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

Inference-time steering of LLMs includes prompt-based control, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. Dense activation steering methods—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, and SAE-based feature steering—share the universal practice of intervening at every generated token; our method departs from it.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to the input to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Activation Addition (ActAdd) computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it to the residual stream at every forward pass. Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) averages over large prompt sets and applies layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, with reduced side effects versus naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors control stylistic attributes; In-Context Vectors extract directions from in-context demonstrations. All apply the steering direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features; SAEs trained on residual stream activations recover interpretable, human-understandable features. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple widths. Amplifying SAE features associated with specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) can steer LLaMA outputs toward those concepts. AxBench benchmarks activation steering methods, comparing effectiveness and side effects. Our work builds on SAE steering but departs from every-token intervention.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step: DExperts combines an expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) model to re-weight token probabilities; PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states; Self-Debiasing suppresses token probabilities from prompted toxic generations; GeDi uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. RealToxicityPrompts shows all such methods incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and shows correction at only a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Concurrent with our work, Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there. SIA is reward-guided decoding: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a value model from trajectory rewards, queries learned guidance during decoding, and uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. Because evaluation protocols differ, results are not directly commensurable; we treat SIA as related work, not a baseline.

Other work argues safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions and focuses steering on initial tokens for weak-to-strong decoding. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text, with a documented trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss, measured standardized across multiple methods. We add the observation that sparse steering improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

These methods intervene in the residual stream at every generated token. Activation Addition (ActAdd) computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it at every forward pass. Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) averages over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions corresponding to concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects versus naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors control stylistic attributes at every decoding step. In-Context Vectors extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations. All apply the steering direction at every generated position; our method departs from this.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features aligning with human-understandable concepts. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for Gemma across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Amplifying SAE features for specific concepts steers LLaMA outputs toward them. AxBench benchmarks activation steering methods, including SAE-based ones, on effectiveness and side effects. We build on SAE steering but do not intervene at every token.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step. DExperts re-weights token probabilities using expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) models. PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states. Self-Debiasing suppresses probabilities of tokens generated under a toxic prompt. GeDi uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. The RealToxicityPrompts benchmark shows all such methods incur fluency cost. We instead use SAE-derived directions applied at only a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

The concurrent Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there. It trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens gives superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a value model, requires auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation, and uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection. We gate a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produce a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. The differing evaluation protocols make results not directly commensurable, so we treat SIA as related work, not a baseline.

Other work argues safety alignment concentrates in early tokens, and weak-to-strong decoding steers initial tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks—mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists under equalized realized budgets is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result is a training-free, position-agnostic control for evaluating selective methods.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text, with a documented trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss. Sparse application improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

\[

\tag{4}

## Abstract

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task‑specific fine‑tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per‑token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gate the signal independently for each token or for a leading window with probability \(p\). Neither method requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation. The optimal steering magnitude increases as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Behavioral control over large language models (LLMs) is essential for reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, or adjusting refusal behavior. Activation steering modifies model behavior by injecting a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream (e.g., Turner et al.). Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide an interpretable basis for such interventions (e.g., Cunningham et al.).  

Standard activation‑steering implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token. Persistent intervention may degrade generation quality. We ask whether dense intervention is necessary. STS samples an independent Bernoulli gate \(m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\) for each token; SBS samples a single gate for a leading window of size \(W\). STS and SBS replace dense steering with sparse, random application governed by a single parameter \(p\). Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full‑steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency‑control trade‑off. Across our experimental settings, the best‑performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 2 Related Work

Activation steering modifies model behavior by adding directions derived from contrastive activations. SAE‑based methods intervene through decoder directions of behavior‑associated sparse features. Prior work applies a fixed intervention at every token; we study sparse application to a subset of tokens.  

## 3 Method

Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be an \(L\)-layer decoder‑only transformer. For a tokenized input \(\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})\), let \(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\) denote the residual‑stream activation at layer \(\ell\) and position \(t\). We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer \(\ell\) :

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}
\]

where \(\mathbf{s}_{t}\) is defined below.  

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

An SAE encoder maps an activation \(\mathbf{h}\) to a sparse feature vector \(f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}\). For positive set \(\mathcal{P}\) and neutral set \(\mathcal{N}\),

\[
\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}
\]

Select the top‑\(K\) features; let \(\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}\). Aggregate into a unit‑norm steering direction

\[
\mathbf{v}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}}{\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert}. \tag{(unnumbered)}
\]

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position \(t\) is

\[
\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}, \qquad \alpha\in\mathbb{R},
\]

where \(m_{t}\in\{0,1\}\) is a binary gate.

#### 3.2.1 Stochastic Token Steering (STS)

For each position \(t\),

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\qquad
m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}
\]

#### 3.2.2 Stochastic Block Steering (SBS)

Sample a single gate \(m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\) per sequence:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}, & t\leq W,\\
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}, & t>W.
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\]

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setup

We evaluated on a toxicity‑reduction task (RealToxicityPrompts) and an emotion‑steering task (GoEmotions). Target emotions: fear and sadness. Models: LLaMA‑3.1‑8B and Gemma‑2‑2B. Steering performed at one intermediate layer. SBS windows: \(W\in\{32,64\}\). Corrective mechanisms: norm preservation, activation clamping, repetition penalty.

### 4.2 Baselines and Metrics

Baselines: No Steering; Full Steering (intervention at every token, \(p=1\)); Prompting (task‑specific safe or emotional instruction). Behavioral metrics: mean toxicity reduction (classifier‑predicted toxicity vs. no steering); mean probability gain (target‑emotion probability vs. unsteered). Generation quality: GPT‑2 perplexity; repetition scores (Rep‑3, Rep‑4).

### 4.3 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Across all settings, most of the behavioral shift is recoverable when only a fraction of tokens are steered. For LLaMA‑3.1‑8B, STS at \(p=0.5\) recovers over 95 % of the full‑steering toxicity reduction and over 75 % of full‑steering gains on both emotion tasks by \(p=0.7\). STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings; on toxicity‑reduction and fear steering on LLaMA‑3.1‑8B it does so at \(p\approx0.5\) or below, whereas on sadness steering for LLaMA‑3.1‑8B the crossover occurs only at \(p\approx0.7\). For Gemma‑2‑2B, prompting remains ahead of STS on sadness steering. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios \(p\), e.g., on fear steering with LLaMA‑3.1‑8B, STS at \(p=0.5\) roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS (\(W=32\)).

### 4.4 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Fluency degradation grows monotonically with steering density: both perplexity and repetition increase as more positions are steered; Full Steering is at the high end. This monotonicity indicates that sparse operating points (below the Full‑Steering ratio) retain lower fluency cost. The required ratio is task dependent; sparse points generally sit below full‑steering cost across SBS window sizes.

### 4.5 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

The best-performing steering magnitude \(\alpha^{*}\) tends to rise as the ratio \(p\) decreases. At a fixed magnitude, behavioral effect increases with \(p\); conversely, the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as \(\alpha\) grows.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS replace dense, every‑token activation steering with a single Bernoulli gating parameter \(p\). Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation behaviors, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full‑steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency‑control trade‑off. ## Limitations

The evaluation covers two tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families. Generalization to other steering targets and decoding settings remains to be validated. The method requires a pretrained SAE with behavior‑relevant features; steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive corpora. Human evaluation is beyond the scope of this work.

The method is designed to reduce harmful generation and shift model behavior toward beneficial targets. It could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors. It requires white‑box access to model activations and a trained SAE; it does not enable new attacks on deployed black‑box systems.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation. Across our experimental settings, the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Standard activation-steering implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token. We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measure the behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios. Dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, and causes less degradation in fluency. The best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, requiring no reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

Prior SAE- and activation-steering methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we study its application to only a subset of token positions. The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requires auxiliary-model queries during decoding, and uses best-of-$N$ generation with reward-model scoring. Our method instead gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, results are not directly comparable (Appendix A).

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Restricting the intervention to a single intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through the remaining layers.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use an SAE trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. Its encoder maps $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, and its decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$, and aggregate them into a unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position; we instead treat the gate as random.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\ m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal. The design is position-agnostic; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit, sampling a single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ once per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on GoEmotions, mapping the fine-grained annotations onto Ekman's basic emotions and taking fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model, we steer with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. We pair every steering method with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding (Appendix C).

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (a task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input, Appendix B). For effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier. For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on three tasks (toxicity reduction, fear and sadness steering). We calibrate the steering magnitude $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below; on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead across the ratios tested. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-3, Rep-4) against intervention ratio for Gemma 2–2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference. Degradation grows monotonically with density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Sparse operating points generally sit below the full-steering cost; the ratio required is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced STS and SBS, two training-free interventions that replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond the scope of this paper. The method requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; interaction with other decoding settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness is unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors (e.g., steering toxicity features in the opposite direction), a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods. However, the methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE and do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts; we do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit and do not collect or release new toxic data. Automated toxicity classifiers (s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier) carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets; we report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth.

## Appendix A Related Work

SIA trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions identified via model entropy, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. It reports that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, inference procedure, and evaluation protocol, so we treat it as related work rather than a baseline. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, a task-dependence that mirrors our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios; whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|} \tag{5}$$

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max}) \tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v} \tag{7}$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Toggling preservation while holding all else fixed (Gemma-2-2B toxicity reduction): enabling it reduces perplexity from roughly $82$ to $30$ and cuts repetition by roughly a factor of three across Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars. The steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the shift intervention induces in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states (Figure 7). Both increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ enlarge this displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens the displacement at each intervened token. The two act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at a fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ is sufficient to recover the effect of denser intervention.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation. The best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: STS recovers most of the full-steering effect steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, adding only an activation vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model, requiring auxiliary-model queries, best-of-$N$ generation, and reward-model scoring. Our method gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion. Given differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, the results are not directly comparable.

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},\tag{1}$$

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

A Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. Encoding a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, we compute the mean activation differential:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).\tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, and aggregate into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We propose two stochastic alternatives.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, sample an independent gate:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).\tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence and applied to a leading window of size $W\leq T$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W.\end{cases}\tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

Two tasks: toxicity reduction (suppression; RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation; GoEmotions, mapped to basic emotions, targeting fear and sadness). Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, each steered with an SAE at an intermediate layer; SBS is evaluated at $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input). Steering effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (RoBERTa toxicity classifier) and mean probability gain (DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier). Generation quality: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$ (fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur).

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Steering magnitude $\alpha$ is calibrated once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and held fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). For LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\approx0.5$ or below; on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\approx0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$); this ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

For Gemma-2-2B on toxicity reduction, both perplexity and repetition (Rep-3, Rep-4) rise monotonically with the fraction of positions steered, with full steering at the high end of both; operating points below the full-steering ratio generally incur lower fluency cost. The required ratio is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than emotion steering), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

The best-performing magnitude $\alpha^{*}$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) tends to rise as the intervention ratio falls: at fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the intervention ratio, and conversely the ratio required for a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. Normalized residual-stream displacement grows with both $\alpha$ and $p$ (Appx. D.3).

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are training-free interventions replacing dense every-token steering with sparse random application governed by $p$. Steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift with an improved fluency-control tradeoff; the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers two behavioral tasks on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may not capture all behavioral dimensions. The method requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive corpora. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interaction with other decoding settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and with sampling-level randomness is unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The same mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors: SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity. The methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE and do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts; no fresh toxic content is generated beyond what the benchmark prompts elicit, and no new toxic data is collected or released. Toxicity classification uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier, whose known biases against identity-related terms may inflate or deflate scores; classifier scores are a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth.

## Appendix A Related Work

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt-based methods are fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Prior methods (ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, DiffMean, Style Vectors, In-Context Vectors) all apply a fixed steering intervention at every generated token; we depart from this.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into more monosemantic features; open checkpoints exist for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths; amplifying behavior-associated features reliably steers outputs. AxBench benchmarks steering methods. Our work departs from the universal every-token intervention practice.

#### Detoxification.

DExperts, PPLM, Self-Debiasing, and GeDi all apply corrections at every decoding step, and RealToxicityPrompts reveals that all incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions applied at only a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

SIA steers only at "critical junctions" identified via model entropy: it trains a token-level value model $V^{*}$ distilled from trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{*})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. It reports that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. It requires auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation, whereas our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion; the differing evaluation protocols make results not directly commensurable.

SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degraded on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2).

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Sparse application of steering improves the fluency–alignment trade-off: by intervening at fewer positions, the residual stream remains closer to its native distribution.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering carries no guarantee that the steered representation remains on the manifold the model decodes fluently; we pair the intervention with three guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

Rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}\tag{5}$$

#### Activation Clamping.

Clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})\tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}\tag{7}$$

The lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

A standard repetition penalty at the decoding stage discounts previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating the guards on a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting: enabling preservation reduces perplexity from roughly 82 to 30 and cuts Rep-3 and Rep-4 by roughly a factor of three, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. Fluency preservation is enabled by default in all reported experiments.

## Abstract  

Activation steering through sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can control large language models (LLMs) without task‑specific fine‑tuning, but dense per‑token intervention introduces constant perturbation that can harm fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), where each token or a leading window is independently steered with probability p. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the dense steering behavioral effect while reducing fluency degradation. Across all experimental settings, the optimal steering magnitude increases as the intervention ratio decreases.

## 1 Introduction  

Large language models require behavioral control for safety, persona alignment, and refusal adjustment. Prompt‑based steering is fragile; output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations and adversarial suffixes. Activation steering injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream, but standard practice applies it at every generated token. We ask whether persistent intervention is necessary. We replace deterministic every‑token steering with stochastic gating and examine the trade‑off between behavioral strength and fluency.

We define Stochastic Token Steering (STS) as independent Bernoulli (p) gating of each token, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) as a single Bernoulli (p) decision applied to a fixed leading window. Both methods require no reward model or learned gating policy, acting only by adding an activation vector during inference.

## 3 Method  

Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be an \(L\)‑layer single‑head decoder‑only transformer.  
For a tokenized input \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_T)\), let \(\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) denote the residual‑stream activation at layer \(\ell\) and position \(t\).  
We inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer \(\ell\):

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + \mathbf{s}_t \quad\text{(1)}
\]

The steering signal \(\mathbf{s}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is defined in §3.2.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE  

A Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) is trained on residual‑stream activations at layer \(\ell\).  
Encoder \(f(\mathbf{h}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{sae}}}\) maps \(\mathbf{h}\) to sparse features; decoder \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}\in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{sae}}\!\times d}\) reconstructs \(\mathbf{h}\).  

Using a positive set \(\mathcal{P}\) exhibiting target behavior and a neutral set \(\mathcal{N}\), we compute the mean differential of feature \(i\):

\[
\Delta_i = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}} f_i(x) - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|} \sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}} f_i(x) \quad\text{(2)}
\]

Select the top‑\(K\) features by \(\Delta_i\), form feature directions \(\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{W}_{\text{dec},i_k}\) for \(k=1,\dots,K\), and aggregate to a unit‑norm steering direction

\[
\mathbf{v} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k}{\Bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k\Bigr\rVert} .
\]

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering  

The signal at position \(t\) is

\[
\mathbf{s}_t = m_t \cdot \alpha \, \mathbf{v},
\]

where \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) is the intervention magnitude, \(\mathbf{v}\) the unit‑norm direction, and \(m_t \in \{0,1\}\) a binary gate.

*Full Steering (FS)* sets \(m_t = 1\) for all positions.  

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS)  

Sample independent gates \(m_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) for each position:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + m_t \, \alpha \mathbf{v}, \qquad
m_t \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p) \quad\text{(3)}
\]

### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS)  

Sample a single gate \(m \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) per sequence and apply it to a leading window of size \(W \le T\):

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} =
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + m \, \alpha \mathbf{v}, & t \le W,\\
\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}, & t > W,
\end{cases} \quad\text{(4)
}
\]

where \(m\) is constant across the window.

## 4 Experiments  

### Setup  

We evaluate on two tasks: toxicity reduction (RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (GoEmotions). Targets: fear and sadness, mapped from fine‑grained Ekman labels. We use LLaMA‑3.1‑8B (EleutherAI/sae‑llama‑3.1‑8b‑32x11) and Gemma‑2‑2B (google/gemma‑scope‑2b, dictionary width 65 K).  

For each model we intervene at a single intermediate layer. SBS window sizes \(W = 32, 64\).  

Steering magnitudes \(\alpha\) are calibrated once under full steering (\(p = 1\)) and then held fixed across all stochastic settings (Figure 5, 6).  

Decoding uses temperature 0.1, repetition penalty 1.1, maximum length 128 tokens. Activation clamping to \([0,40]\) is applied. Norm preservation and repetition penalty constitute fluency‑preserving regularization (Appendix C.1).  

Each experiment uses 300 prompts for emotion discovery, 600 toxic prompts for toxicity discovery, and 300 neutral prompts for emotion evaluation.  

### Baselines and Metrics  

*No Steering* – unmodified generation.  
*Full Steering* – intervention at every token, \(p=1\).  
*Prompting* – task‑specific safety or emotion instruction prepended (Appendix B).  

Behavioral effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (difference in RoBERTa toxicity classifier scores) and mean target‑emotion probability gain (DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier).  
Fluency: GPT‑2 perplexity and repetition scores (Rep‑3, Rep‑4).

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness  

Figure 1 shows behavioral gain over no steering versus intervention ratio \(p\).  

Table 1 (below) reports the behavioral shift for LLaMA‑3.1‑8B and Gemma‑2‑2B under matched intervention ratios. For LLaMA‑3.1‑8B, STS with \(p=0.5\) recovers over 95 % of full‑steering toxicity reduction; \(p=0.7\) recovers over 75 % of full‑steering gains on both emotion tasks. STS outperforms prompting in five of six model–task settings; for fear on LLaMA‑3.1‑8B, STS overtakes prompting already by \(p \approx 0.5\). SBS produces smaller behavioral shifts at equivalent \(p\).  

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering  

Figure 2 reports perplexity and Rep‑3, Rep‑4 versus intervention ratio for Gemma‑2‑2B (toxicity). Both metrics increase monotonically as more tokens are steered; dense steering (\(p=1\)) lies at the high end.  

Sparse intervention ratios generally incur lower fluency cost than dense steering while achieving comparable behavioral shift. SBS yields similar fluency to STS but with reduced behavioral effect at matched \(p\).

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio  

Figure 3 plots the best‑performing steering magnitude \(\alpha^{*}\) (maximizing behavioral shift with fluency preservation) against the intervention ratio. The optimal \(\alpha^{*}\) rises as \(p\) falls across both models and tasks. At a fixed \(\alpha\), behavioral effect increases with \(p\); conversely, a larger \(\alpha\) can compensate for sparser intervention.

## 5 Conclusion  

STS and SBS provide training‑free, inference‑time interventions that replace dense per‑token activation steering with sparse random application controlled by a single parameter \(p\). Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the dense steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency‑control trade‑off. The best‑performing steering magnitude grows as intervention ratio falls.  

---  

## Limitations  

Evaluation is limited to toxicity reduction and emotion steering on LLaMA‑3.1‑8B and Gemma‑2‑2B. Generalization to other behaviors (hallucination, persona enforcement, multi‑attribute control) remains untested. Classifier‑based behavior assessment may not capture all dimensions; human evaluation would strengthen findings. SAE‑based steering relies on pretrained dictionaries and contrastive corpora; steering quality depends on dictionary quality. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, or beam search are unexplored.

## Intended use and dual‑use considerations  

The method offers training‑free inference‑time behavioral control aimed at reducing harmful generation and encouraging beneficial behaviors. Inverting the steering direction could amplify harmful behaviors; however, this requires white‑box access to model activations and a pretrained SAE, and cannot be applied to deployed black‑box systems.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation, and the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Standard activation-steering implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token. We ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating. STS samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position; SBS draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site. Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens and causing less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, adding only an activation vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

Existing activation-steering and SAE-based methods apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we study its application to only a subset of token positions. The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding, best-of-$N$ generation, and reward-model scoring. Our method instead gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given the differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, the reported results are not directly comparable.

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$

where the steering signal $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing at an intermediate layer allows the signal to propagate through the remaining layers.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use an SAE trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$. The SAE decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$ and form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, where $i_{k}$ indexes the $k$-th selected feature. We aggregate these into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.
