### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ takes the form $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ is the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate. The standard approach, Full Steering (FS), sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We instead treat the gate as a random variable, controlling the fraction of steered positions and thereby trading off behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\quad m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal. This position-agnostic design makes no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant. The parameter $p$ interpolates smoothly between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\ \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate on two tasks spanning opposite intervention goals: toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on GoEmotions, mapping fine-grained annotations onto basic emotions and taking fear and sadness as targets. We use two open-weight models from distinct families and scales, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model, we steer with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer, and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the model's native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, we pair every steering method with three lightweight corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: (1) No Steering (unmodified generation), (2) Full Steering (intervention at every token, $p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (a curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input). For steering effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier. For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on three tasks. We calibrate the steering magnitude $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios. Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$, confirming that the majority of per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, and on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$; the exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across the ratios we test. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-$3$, Rep-$4$) against intervention ratio for Gemma 2–2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference. Degradation grows monotonically with density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Operating points below the full-steering ratio generally incur lower fluency cost. The ratio required is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced STS and SBS, two training-free interventions that replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond the scope of this short paper. Our method inherits the limitations of SAE-based steering: it requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; how stochastic steering interacts with other decoding settings (e.g. higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) remains unexplored, as does the interaction between gate-level randomness and sampling-level randomness.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This training-free method for inference-time behavioral control could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors: SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods. However, the methods studied here require white-box access to model activations and to a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Our toxicity reduction experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, released under terms that permit such use. We do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit, and we do not collect or release new toxic data. Automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth.

## Appendix A Related Work

Dense activation steering methods (ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE-based feature steering, DiffMean, Style Vectors, In-Context Vectors) share the practice of intervening at every generated token; our method departs from it. Prompt-based control is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions. Existing detoxification methods (DExperts, PPLM, Self-Debiasing, GeDi) apply corrections at every decoding step and incur some fluency cost. The concurrent SIA identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy, trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines, reporting that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that SBS underperforms STS at matched nominal ratios; whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering carries no guarantee that the resulting representation remains on the manifold the model decodes fluently; drift manifests as degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, and repetitive generations. We pair the intervention with three guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the norm of the original:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|} \tag{5}$$

This constrains the intervention to rotate the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to a range $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max}) \tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v} \tag{7}$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range, while the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses any residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering suppresses high-probability continuations, which can drive the model toward repetitive sequences. We apply a standard repetition penalty at the decoding stage, discounting previously generated tokens without further modifying the hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating preservation on a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting (Figure 4), enabling preservation reduces perplexity substantially (from roughly $82$ to $30$) and cuts repetition roughly by a factor of three across both Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

We measure the shift that intervention induces in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between the steered and unsteered hidden states (Figure 7). The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_i(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$. The SAE decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute:

$$\Delta_i=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$ and form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$. We aggregate into a single unit-norm steering direction:

$$\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k\Big/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k\bigr\rVert.$$

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ takes the form $\mathbf{s}_t=m_t\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ is the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_t\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ at every position.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_t\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal. The parameter $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate on two tasks: toxicity reduction (suppression, built on RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation, built on GoEmotions, targeting fear and sadness per Ekman's basic emotions). We use LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model, we steer with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (task-specific instruction prepended to input). For steering effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction and mean probability gain (target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier. For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$ (fraction of $n$-grams that recur).

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

We calibrate $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios. For LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below; on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across all tested ratios. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

For Gemma 2-2B on toxicity reduction, both perplexity and repetition rise monotonically with steering density, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Sparse operating points sit below the full-steering cost. The trend holds across SBS window sizes.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

The best-performing steering magnitude $\alpha^*$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) tends to rise as the intervention ratio falls. At a fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the steering ratio; conversely the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced STS and SBS, two training-free interventions that replace dense every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency–control tradeoff. The best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks on two model families. Generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation would strengthen the findings. Our method inherits the limitations of SAE-based steering: it requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; interaction with other decoding settings (e.g., higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness remains unexplored.

The same mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors (e.g., steering SAE features identified for toxicity reduction in the opposite direction). This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

We use RealToxicityPrompts, a dataset constructed for research on toxic language. We do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit. ### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the norm of the original:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\bigr\|} \tag{5}$$

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max}) \tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v} \tag{7}$$

The lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ actively suppresses any residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at the decoding stage, discounting previously generated tokens.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

On a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting, enabling preservation reduces perplexity from roughly 82 to 30 and cuts repetition roughly by a factor of three across both Rep-3 and Rep-4 metrics, with non-overlapping error bars. The behavioral steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

STS and SBS are training-free Bernoulli gates for SAE steering; neither requires a reward model or a learned gating policy.

## 1 Introduction

We ask how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS). The method is training-free, uses a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, and adds only an activation-vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

SIA is treated as related work rather than an experimental baseline.

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},
\tag{1}
\]

where the steering signal $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. We restrict the intervention to a single intermediate layer. Editing the residual stream there allows the signal to propagate through the remaining layers, so the model can integrate it before generating the next token.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ to identify directions associated with a target behavior. The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$. The SAE decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. To isolate behavior-discriminative features, we encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

\[
\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).
\tag{2}
\]

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$ and form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, where $i_{k}$ indexes the $k$-th selected feature. We aggregate these into a single unit-norm steering direction

\[
\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert,
\]

so that features are combined in proportion to how strongly they distinguish the target behavior.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ takes the form

\[
\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},
\]

where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ is the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate that decides whether position $t$ is steered. The standard approach, Full Steering (FS), sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We instead treat the gate as a random variable, controlling the fraction of steered positions and thereby trading behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).
\tag{3}
\]

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal while the rest are left unperturbed. This position-agnostic design makes no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant. The parameter $p$ interpolates smoothly between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,
\end{cases}
\tag{4}
\]

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate two tasks spanning opposite intervention goals: toxicity reduction, a suppression task on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task on GoEmotions. Emotion steering maps GoEmotions annotations onto basic emotions and uses fear and sadness as targets. We use two open-weight models from distinct families and scales, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model, we steer with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer. We evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Additive steering can displace activations off the native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, so we pair every steering method with norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: No Steering (unmodified generation), Full Steering (intervention at every token, $p{=}1$), and Prompting (a carefully curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input; Appendix B.1). For steering effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction, the decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering, and mean probability gain, the increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation. Toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C). For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports behavioral gain over no steering for STS and SBS across intervention ratio $p$ on toxicity reduction, fear steering, and sadness steering, with dashed baselines for prompting, full steering, and no steering, and shaded standard-deviation bands. To ensure a fair comparison, we calibrate the steering magnitude $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost. For LLaMA-3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. This indicates that the majority of per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings. On toxicity reduction for both models and on fear steering for LLaMA-3.1-8B, it does so by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, i.e. while leaving at least half of the tokens unperturbed. On sadness steering for LLaMA-3.1-8B, the crossover occurs only at higher ratios, $p\!\approx\!0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across the ratios we test. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA-3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4) against intervention ratio for Gemma-2 2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference and shaded standard-deviation bands. Degradation grows monotonically with steering density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both metrics. This monotonicity makes sparsity useful: operating points below the full-steering ratio generally have lower fluency cost. The required ratio is task dependent, smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering. Sparse operating points generally sit below the full-steering cost, and the trend holds across SBS window sizes, so it is not a method-specific artifact.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Figure 3 plots best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ for GoEmotions-fear against intervention ratio $p$ for both models; at each $p$, $\alpha^{*}$ maximizes target-emotion probability gain subject to fluency preservation. The best-performing steering magnitude tends to rise as the ratio falls. Empirically, at a fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the steering intervention ratio, and conversely the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as the per-token strength grows. Appendix D.3 shows that the normalized residual-stream displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

## 5 Conclusion

Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families. These span suppression and elicitation, but generalization to other steering targets, such as hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, and multi-attribute control, remains unvalidated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation would strengthen the findings but is beyond the scope of this short paper. Our method inherits the limitations of SAE-based steering: it requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; how stochastic steering interacts with other decoding settings, such as higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, and beam search, remains unexplored, and the interaction between gate-level randomness and sampling-level randomness is a natural direction for future work.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This work develops a training-free method for inference-time behavioral control of language models, with the primary motivation of reducing harmful generation, such as toxicity, and shifting model behavior toward beneficial targets, such as emotional regulation. The same mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors: SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity. This dual-use concern is shared by activation-steering methods. However, the methods studied here require white-box access to model activations and to a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We believe the net effect of advancing interpretable, training-free behavioral control is positive, particularly in deployment settings where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Our toxicity reduction experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, a dataset constructed specifically for research on toxic language and released under terms that permit such use. We do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit, and we do not collect or release new toxic data. Toxicity classifications use s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier. Automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth about whether specific outputs are harmful.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs that include toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, to provide an honest qualitative characterization of the method, including its failure modes. These examples are prefaced by content warnings in both the appendix and at the front of the paper. We have excluded examples containing identity-targeted slurs, even where the benchmark prompts would have elicited them, because the marginal scientific value of including them does not outweigh the harm of reproducing such content in print. ## Appendix A Related Work

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt-based steering is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override safety instructions, and steerability through prompting is asymmetric and bounded.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Dense activation steering methods apply a steering direction at every generated token; our method applies the signal to a subset of token positions.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into sparser, more monosemantic features, and selected decoder directions can be amplified to steer behavior.

#### Detoxification.

Our detoxification task uses RealToxicityPrompts and applies an SAE-derived direction to a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention by identifying critical junctions via model entropy and steering only at those positions. It is a reward-guided decoding method: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. It reports that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA trains a separate value model from trajectory rewards, queries learned guidance during decoding, and reports reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection. These components require auxiliary-model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method instead gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and produces a single completion. Because the methods differ in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, their reported results are not directly comparable. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, a task-dependence that mirrors SBS underperforming STS at matched nominal $p$; whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). STS is a training-free, position-agnostic control for evaluating selective methods.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Sparse application can improve the fluency–alignment tradeoff by keeping the residual stream closer to its native distribution.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

The additive intervention can drift in norm or direction away from natural activations and degrade fluency, inflate perplexity, and cause repetition. We therefore use lightweight guards that keep the steered activation close to the model’s natural operating regime while leaving the intended behavioral effect intact.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the norm of the original:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}
\tag{5}
\]

This constrains the intervention to rotate the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude, preserving the scale invariants assumed by downstream computations.

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to a range $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

\[
s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})
\tag{6}
\]

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}
\tag{7}
\]

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature’s natural range, while the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ actively suppresses any residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering can suppress high-probability continuations and cause repetitive sequences. We apply a standard repetition penalty at the decoding stage, discounting previously generated tokens without further modifying the hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

We ablate the guards on a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting, comparing Preserve ON with Preserve OFF while holding all other settings fixed. Figure 4 reports the results, with error bars denoting standard deviation across generations. Enabling preservation reduces perplexity from roughly $82$ to $30$ and cuts Rep-3 and Rep-4 repetition by roughly a factor of three, with non-overlapping standard-deviation error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral steering effect is applied identically in both conditions, so the improvements reflect the guards keeping generation on the natural manifold rather than weakening the steering signal. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

## Abstract

STS and SBS gate SAE activation steering sparsely with a Bernoulli probability $p$.

## 1 Introduction

Activation steering via SAEs controls LLM behavior without task-specific fine-tuning; dense per-token steering risks fluency degradation. Behavioral control includes reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, and adjusting refusal. Prompt steering is fragile: minor lexical perturbation shifts outputs, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream. SAEs decompose activations into sparse features; amplified decoder directions promote or suppress behavior. Standard steering applies the direction at every generated token; stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation.

STS samples independent gates $m_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at each position; SBS draws one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence for a leading window. Across two model families and suppression/elicitation tasks, STS recovers most full-steering effect on a token fraction with less fluency degradation. Best steering magnitude rises as intervention ratio falls. The method uses one sparsity parameter $p$, no reward model or learned gating policy, and only an activation-vector addition.

## 2 Related Work

SIA is the closest concurrent work; Appendix A details the comparison.

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$, let $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. Inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}.
\]

The intervention is restricted to a single intermediate layer.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

A SAE at layer $\ell$ has encoder $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$; $f_i(\mathbf{h})$ is feature $i$ activation. Decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. Encode positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and neutral set $\mathcal{N}$:

\[
\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).
\]

Select top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$; set $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$. Aggregate

\[
\mathbf{v}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}}{\left\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\right\rVert},
\]

a unit-norm direction combining features proportionally to their discriminative strength.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ is unit-norm, and $m_t\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ at every position. Stochastic gates control the steered fraction and trade behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, sample $m_t \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).
\]

In expectation, fraction $p$ is steered. The design is position-agnostic. $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ is atomic. Sample one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:

\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v} & t\leq W,\\
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)} & t>W.
\end{cases}
\]

With probability $p$ the window is steered; with probability $1-p$ it is intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

Tasks are toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on GoEmotions. Emotion steering maps fine-grained annotations onto basic emotions, with fear and sadness as targets. Models are LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, from distinct families and scales. Each model uses an SAE at an intermediate layer; SBS is evaluated at $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method uses norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: No Steering (unmodified generation), Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and Prompting (carefully curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended; Appendix B). Effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (classifier-predicted decrease relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (target-emotion probability increase relative to unsteered generation). Toxicity uses a RoBERTa classifier; emotion uses a DistilRoBERTa classifier (Appendix C). Quality: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$, the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 measures STS and SBS effectiveness versus intervention ratio $p$ as behavioral gain over no steering, with static prompting, full-steering, and no-steering baselines and standard-deviation bands. $\alpha$ is calibrated once at full steering ($p{=}1$) and held fixed. Most behavioral shift is recoverable at reduced cost: LLaMA 3.1-8B STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction; by $p{=}0.7$ it recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks. Thus most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant.

STS overtakes prompting in five of six model–task settings. On toxicity reduction (both models) and fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, it does so by $p\approx0.5$ or below, leaving at least half of tokens unperturbed; on sadness for LLaMA 3.1-8B, crossover is $p\approx0.7$. Exception: sadness on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead across tested ratios. Surpassing prompting while perturbing only a fraction of positions indicates the behavioral signal need not be present at every step.

STS yields larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal $p$, clearest on emotion: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles SBS ($W{=}32$) probability gain. This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 shows that for Gemma 2–2B toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference, perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 rise monotonically with steering density; full steering is at the high end. This monotonicity makes sparsity useful: lower-ratio operating points generally have lower fluency cost. Required ratio is task-dependent, smaller for toxicity reduction than emotion steering, and the trend holds across SBS window sizes, so it is not a method-specific artifact.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Figure 3 plots best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) versus intervention ratio for GoEmotions-fear; at each $p$, $\alpha^{*}$ maximizes target-emotion probability gain subject to fluency preservation. $\alpha^{*}$ tends to rise as ratio falls. At fixed $\alpha$, behavioral effect increases with intervention ratio; conversely, the ratio required for a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. Appendix D.3 shows normalized residual-stream displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

## 5 Conclusion

Effective inference-time behavioral control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families. Generalization to hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, and multi-attribute control is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond the scope of this short paper. The method requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive corpora. Experiments use one decoding configuration; interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, and beam search are unexplored, as is the interaction between gate-level and sampling-level randomness.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This work provides training-free inference-time behavioral control, primarily to reduce harmful generation such as toxicity and shift behavior toward beneficial targets such as emotional regulation. The mechanism can be inverted to amplify harmful behavior, e.g., by steering toxicity-reduction SAE features oppositely. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods and is not specific here. The methods require white-box access to activations and a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. The net effect is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, released for research on toxic language. No fresh toxic content is generated beyond what benchmark prompts naturally elicit, and no new toxic data are collected or released. Toxicity classifications use s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers have known biases against identity-related terms and may inflate or deflate affected scores. Scores are a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs containing toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, with content warnings in the appendix and at the front. These examples provide a qualitative characterization, including failure modes. Identity-targeted slurs are excluded even where benchmark prompts would elicit them.

## Appendix A Related Work

SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention by identifying critical junctions via model entropy and steering only at those positions. It trains a token-level value model $V^{*}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{*})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. It reports that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA requires auxiliary-model queries, auxiliary model storage, and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. The methods differ in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, so results are not directly comparable.

SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrades on helpfulness tasks; this mirrors SBS underperforming STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists when realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). STS is a training-free, position-agnostic control for evaluating selective methods. Sparse application improves the fluency–alignment tradeoff by keeping the residual stream closer to its native distribution.
